https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text: The Westconnex, which alone accounted for 359,000 trips a day by the end of 2025, will not get a toll reduction. Photograph: NSW Government View image in fullscreen The Westconnex, which alone accounted for 359,000 trips a day by the end of 2025, will not get a toll reduction. Photograph: NSW Government Transport Most Sydney road tolls to keep rising after Transurban accused of blocking reforms Handful of tollroads to get one-off price cuts but WestConnex toll to keep rising at least 4% a year Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Luca Ittimani Mon 3 Aug 2026 11.00 EDT Last modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 11.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The cost of using Sydney’s biggest toll road will continue to rise at least 4% a year after the multinational private operator was accused of blocking the state government’s push for sweeping reforms. Only a handful of Sydney’s motorways will receive one-off toll cuts under a deal announced by the state Labor government on Monday, as the tolling bill footed by taxpayers surpasses $1bn. Eleven of Sydney’s toll roads are run by Transurban, a $47bn company with operations in Victoria, Queensland and the US, with most under contracts granting exclusive operating rights into the 2040s or later. The deal will see the state pay $850m to widen the M2-M7 tollway, boosting traffic flows, which Transurban expects will increase its toll revenue. The government will separately spend $143m to settle the deal, negotiated over two years. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Under Monday’s deal, Transurban will cut some fares by 10% on the Lane Cove Tunnel and the M2 in July 2027 and the M7 in 2028. The cross-city tunnel toll will be cut by a one-off 20% in 2028 while the eastern distributor’s northbound fare will be cut and a southbound fare added. Those highways accounted for less than half of the 1m trips recorded each day on average across Transurban’s Sydney network, suggesting most tollway trips would not see a toll reduction. EVs and hybrids approach half of Australian new car sales amid ongoing fuel crisis Read more The Westconnex highway, which alone accounted for 359,000 trips a day by the end of 2025, and the NorthConnex will not get a reduction. The premier, Chris Minns , told reporters on Monday the government had failed to negotiate a deal for the excluded highways at an appropriate cost with Transurban. “We weren’t able to get the rate of the dollars that we wanted in exchange for, I guess, what we had to give up,” Minns said. “We need toll relief now and it’s better to have it at a lower base given the multiple increases that they have through the year.” Transurban’s chief executive, Michelle Jablko, told investors on Monday the state would have had to spend significant amounts to fund a WestConnex toll reduction. “Even a small change in WestConnex could cost taxpayers quite a lot,” Jablko said. Transurban data indicates the average Sydney customer spends nearly $650 a year on tolls. It costs $12.74 for a car to travel the full length of WestConnex and the motorway’s tolls increase by at least 4% each year. Allan Fels, a former chief of the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission, led the state’s 2024 tolling review and called for the different roads’ tolls to be standardised so toll burdens would be balanced between Sydney’s west and its wealthier north and east. Jabklo on Monday said sweeping reforms could worsen congestion. Fels, who was not directly involved in the government’s negotiations, said Monday’s toll reductions represented a “good start”. But he said Transurban had blocked reform and put profits over public interest. The company declined to comment. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks Preview latest after newsletter promotion “It’s essentially a financial vehicle, that receives an enormous amount of money, and that’s what it’s all about,” Fels told Guardian Australia. “[Transurban’s demands] were excessive, completely out of the ballpark … Their whole approach to compensation ruled out some public interest reforms, including on WestConnex.” NSW taxpayers already pay Transurban more than $100m a year to cover Labor’s cap on tolls introduced in January 2024, covering the difference for motorists spending more than $60 each week. That figure will more than double to $211m in 2026-27 after the state budget temporarily lowered the cap to $50. Fels said commuter anger at growing toll bills would force the state to revisit the contracts in future. “The government deemed it was just too tough politically in the face of resistance by Transurban to deliver the whole package … [but] they hinted they might come back to this,” he said. Jablko did not directly answer when asked on Monday whether the government had promised it would not amend the contracts in future. “By working constructively with the government, we were able to deal into what was important to them today and protect the value of the contracts,” she said. “What government wants to do in the future is always going to be a question for them, but it was really important for us to show up in the right way.” Explore more on these topics Transport Sydney New South Wales Chris Minns New South Wales politics news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

https://telex.hu/belfold/2026/09/03/magy.text: Menü Kereső Magyar Pétert a Sándor-palotában fogadta Baka András Belföld frissítve Iván-Nagy Szilvia Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom Tájékoztatást nyújtott Baka András köztársasági elnöknek Magyar Péter a Tisza-kormány eddig elért eredményeiről és az előttük álló feladatokról – számolt be a miniszterelnök a Facebook-oldalán arról, hogy munkaegyeztetésen járt a Sándor-palotában. „Hosszan egyeztettünk a kormány által képviselt külpolitikai irányról. Megköszöntem elnök úrnak, hogy a külügyminiszter asszonnyal együtt képviseli Magyarországot az ENSZ soron következő közgyűlésén” – írta Magyar. A találkozó után a Sándor-palota Facebook-oldala azt írta, hogy Magyarország állami berendezkedésének egyik alapja, hogy a hatalmi ágak önállóan, de együttműködésben végzik feladatukat. A kormány és az államfő munkája számos esetben, például a diplomácia vagy a közjog területén is kiegészíti egymást. „Baka András köztársasági elnök négyszemközti munkamegbeszélésen fogadta Magyar Péter miniszterelnököt a Sándor-palotában. Egyeztetésükön a következő időszakban várható programok és tervek kerültek előtérbe, mint például a szeptember egyik kiemelt külpolitikai eseményének számító New York-i ENSZ Közgyűlés, amelyen Magyarország képviseletében az államfő fog felszólalni” – írt az államfő hivatala. A miniszterelnök első alkalommal járt Baka Andrásnál a Sándor-palotában azóta, hogy Baka augusztus 19-én hivatalba lépett . Az Országgyűlés 140 szavazattal választotta meg a Tisza Párt jelöltjét, aki korábban az Emberi Jogok Európai Bíróságának bírája és a Legfelsőbb Bíróság elnöke volt. Az eskütétele után arról beszélt, hogy államfőként azon szeretne dolgozni, hogy a különböző érdekű és meggyőződésű emberek békésen tudjanak együtt élni, és a vitáikat ne erővel, hanem szabályozott keretek között rendezzék. Sulyok Tamás korábbi elnököt az áprilisban megválasztott Tisza-kormány bábnak tartotta, és már a választási kampányban jelezte, hogy nem maradhat hivatalban. A tiszás többségű parlament július 13-án megszavazta azt az Alaptörvény-módosítást, ami lehetővé tette a köztársasági elnök elmozdítását. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.text: Ukraine’s former prosecutor general, Ruslan Kravchenko, gives a press conference in Kyiv in July. Photograph: Thomas Peter/Reuters View image in fullscreen Ukraine’s former prosecutor general, Ruslan Kravchenko, gives a press conference in Kyiv in July. Photograph: Thomas Peter/Reuters Ukraine Ukraine’s prosecutor general quits after anti-corruption agents raid his office Ruslan Kravchenko resigns over allegations some of his officials were engaged in large-scale money laundering Luke Harding in London and Amy Hawkins in Kharkiv Tue 8 Sep 2026 13.00 EDT Last modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 15.15 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Ukraine’s prosecutor general has resigned after investigators used ladders to raid his office in connection with a major corruption scandal that threatens to embarrass Volodymyr Zelenskyy. Ruslan Kravchenko quit his post on Monday after allegations that some of his officials were involved in large-scale money laundering. They received cash to protect call centres involved in illegal phone scams, it was claimed. Kravchenko, who denies wrongdoing, left his job after meeting Zelenskyy. Ukraine’s president also spoke to the heads of Nabu and Sapo, the two anti-corruption agencies that have uncovered a sprawling criminal scheme involving government officials. Zelenskyy described his conversation with Kravchenko as “fairly long” and said: “I’m sure you understand what we discussed.” The prosecutor’s resignation letter will be sent to Ukraine’s parliament, the Verkhovna Rada, he said. Kravchenko is the latest member of Zelenskyy’s inner circle to be linked to corruption. The allegations involve so-called call centres operating in Ukraine. Employees pose as banks, law enforcement agencies or investment advisers, and persuade victims to transfer funds to accounts or crypto wallets under their control. Those targeted include Ukrainians, Russians and EU citizens. According to Nabu, a senior official inside the prosecutor general’s office protected the criminal network and helped it to launder its assets. Each “call centre” paid $7,000 (£5,200) a month in protection money, law enforcement sources told the Ukrainska Pravda newspaper . The bribes ran into millions of dollars, it said, with hundreds of centres believed to employ about 60,000 people across the country. Nabu investigators raided Kravchenko’s office on Friday. Staff refused to let them in so they used ladders to scale a metal gate. Kravchenko was not at work and had disappeared from his home, which was searched later that evening. The chief suspect was arrested in the western city of Lviv. Recordings of phone calls published by Nabu suggested he was overseeing repairs at Kravchenko’s home while simultaneously collecting bribes from the fraudulent call centres. Nabu released images over the weekend of a safe filled with bundles of dollar bills. It said it had uncovered five officials behind the scheme but did not name them. The cash was spent on real estate, jewellery and other valuables, it said, laying out its evidence in a 30-minute video . Zelenskyy tried to strip Nabu and Sapo of their independence last year, a move he reversed after protests in Kyiv and other cities. There are further claims that the prosecutor’s office subsequently spied on Nabu staff and tried to obstruct their work. The revelations come at a time when Ukraine is under day-and-night attack from Russian drones and missiles. Three people were killed and 19 injured in overnight strikes on Kyiv that caused huge fires and left smoke hanging over the city. The onslaught marked the end of a three-day ceasefire in the capital after a visit on Sunday by Donald Trump’s envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. They visited Moscow on Saturday and met Vladimir Putin. Zelenskyy said the pair had brought some “very good, worthwhile ideas” for ending the war but gave no further details. He said he hoped to meet Trump in the next two weeks. Few expect a breakthrough, with the Kremlin claiming on Tuesday that its forces were close to victory. While Russia escalated its bombing, Ukrainians were talking about corruption investigations, posting numerous comments on social media, the transparency advocate Olena Tregub said. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion “Society is shocked and appalled by government officials who are basically behaving as mafia,” she said. “It’s not even corruption. It’s organised crime, protecting illegal call centres that were scamming people, not only in Ukraine but in Europe .” She said anti-corruption investigations were different from previous ones because Nabu detectives were “very good technically”. “They are recording people in their homes, in their offices and over the phone,” she said. “They are outsmarting other law enforcement bodies fighting against them, and are able to tape people who think everything is discreet.” She said the high-profile raids were “changing the culture in Ukraine” and making society less tolerant of ill-gotten wealth. Zelenskyy’s former business partner fled the country last year after being implicated in a corruption case featuring the state nuclear energy company . Two ministers were fired . The president’s powerful chief of staff, Andriy Yermak, also later resigned after being questioned. Both deny wrongdoing. Kravchenko rejected the allegations against him on Sunday, calling them “completely unsubstantiated”. A day later he said he did not want his office “to be used as a tool in political confrontation”. The deputy chair of parliament’s law enforcement committee, Andriy Osadchuk, said the ​scandal underlined the need to ‌reform the prosecution service ​and called for key posts ​to be filled through open competition. Fighting corruption was also vital to Kyiv’s bid for EU membership, he said. “It will be very difficult for Ukraine to move forward if we do not change the approach to selecting and appointing the prosecutor general and prosecutors at lower levels,” Osadchuk said. https://hungarytoday.hu/4ig-enters-energ.text: 4iG Enters Energy Sector with Plans for Regional Expansion 4iG is establishing a new energy business and a separate holding company to build it out, further expanding its presence in the critical infrastructure sector, the Budapest-based company said in a statement on Thursday. The company has signed a letter of intent with U.S.-based X-ENERGY for the regional deployment of small modular nuclear reactors (SMRs), reached a preliminary cooperation agreement to acquire a wind farm in Poland, and is also exploring opportunities to develop wind power and energy storage capacity in North Macedonia and Montenegro. 4iG plans to bring long-term international investment and technology partners into the development of its portfolio, with the dual objectives of acquiring operating power-generation assets, developing new capacity, and introducing next-generation energy technologies to the region. The strategic fit of the energy business is further strengthened by the fact that 4iG’s core activities are concentrated in energy-intensive sectors, reads the statement. Building and acquiring its own power-generation capacity could therefore create significant advantages for the group’s existing businesses, reduce its exposure to energy costs over the long term, and make its energy supply more predictable, the company noted. As a first major step toward strengthening the long-term energy security and reducing energy dependence of Central and Eastern Europe and the Western Balkans, 4iG has signed a letter of intent with U.S.-based X-ENERGY for the regional deployment of small modular nuclear reactors (SMRs). The company added that the 4iG Group has also reached a preliminary cooperation agreement to acquire a medium-sized, turnkey wind farm in Poland. Due diligence on the project is currently underway. The group is exploring opportunities to develop wind power and related energy storage capacity in North Macedonia, where 4iG is currently working on the rollout of its 5G mobile network and plans to launch its telecommunications services in 2027. More than 500 5G base stations will be built over four years. Continue reading The group is also exploring opportunities to acquire additional power-generation capacity in Montenegro with the involvement of partners. 4iG’s existing business presence in the Western Balkans provides a regional platform on which the further expansion of its energy business can be built. The company also reported on the Budapest Stock Exchange website that its wholly owned subsidiary, 4iG Investment Ltd., will submit a binding offer to acquire the investment units of the iG Tech Energy private equity fund. This is the first step in a multi-stage transaction that, once completed, could enable 4iG to directly acquire the project company owned by the fund. The project company holds a 49 percent stake in a portfolio of wind farms operating at five sites in northwestern Hungary, with a combined capacity of 158 MW. The portfolio accounts for nearly half of Hungary’s total installed wind power capacity. 4iG Plc. employs 11,000 people. BBC's James Landale explains why the incident could signal an escalation in Russia's war against Ukraine. More on this story here. https://www.rfi.fr/en/podcasts/internati.text: International report Shipping attacks threaten Turkey's resolve to keep warships out of Black Sea Issued on: 17/10/2026 - 13:43 Play - 06:36 A wave of deadly attacks on cargo ships in the waters of NATO members Bulgaria and Romania has jolted the alliance into calling an emergency meeting on Black Sea security. Yet any move to send NATO ships hinges on Turkey reversing its steadfast refusal to allow warships into the Black Sea. A cargo ship that was attacked in the Black Sea is escorted by a coastguard boat as it returns through the Bosphorus in Istanbul, Turkey, on 1 September 2026. © Murad Sezer / Reuters Advertising Thursday saw two chemical tankers struck by drones close to a Romanian port. It follows two similar attacks in Bulgarian waters in the past week. More than 20 sailors have been killed or remain missing. “The war has come in full force to the Black Sea now,” said Yoruk Isik, a maritime analyst who runs the Istanbul-based Bosphorus Observer consultancy. “With the change in technology compared to the beginning of the war, drones really disrupted maritime traffic.” According to Isik, the latest attacks underscore the growing spread of the conflict between Russia and Ukraine. “Russian ports and Ukrainian ports are heavily targeted, but now even in NATO waters ships are getting hit, in Bulgarian waters, Romanian waters. “We are at a point where there is no safe place.” The latest strikes targeted vessels along a key Ukrainian shipping route, casting Russia as NATO’s prime suspect as Moscow intensifies its assault on Ukrainian trade. After meeting on Thursday with the leaders of Bulgaria and Romania, both NATO members, Secretary-General Mark Rutte said the military alliance would “continue to work closely with our allies in the Black Sea, adjusting our deterrence and defence posture as needed”. Romanian President Nicușor Dan said NATO would hold a crisis meeting next week to discuss the situation. Gatekeeper to the Black Sea NATO could deploy air defence systems against drones to protect Bulgarian and Romanian waters. But any deployment of naval ships will depend on NATO member Turkey, which controls access to the Black Sea through the Turkish Straits under a long-standing international treaty, the 1936 Montreux Convention . Since Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, Ankara has blocked entry of Russian and Ukrainian warships or military vessels belonging to NATO members without a Black Sea coast, arguing for a diplomatic solution. In recent weeks the Turkish government has sought to broker a ceasefire on commercial shipping, without success. Isik claims that failure, coupled with the latest escalation in attacks, is increasingly calling into question Ankara’s reliance on diplomacy alone. “Either they’re going to have a breakthrough and the Kremlin is going to de-escalate, or Ankara is going to accept the reality that there needs to be a more credible force here – bigger vessels have to come,” the analyst said. He pointed out that the navies of Romania and Bulgaria are not equipped to handle such an operation alone, with Cold War-era ships nearing the end of their lifespan. “So Turkey's engagement is key to any successful NATO planning in the Black Sea.” Russian leverage Despite Turkish-owned cargo ships coming under attack in recent weeks, and Turkey’s deep reliance on Black Sea trade, Ankara has so far kept its powerful navy on the sidelines. International relations expert Huseyin Bagci, of Ankara’s Middle East Technical University, says Turkey fears an escalation in the conflict and will be wary of allowing NATO ships into the Black Sea. “I do not think the government would dare,” said Bagci. “Probably the government considers this a provocation to drag Turkey into the war... Turkey is afraid of getting involved in the Black Sea against Russia, this is somehow a trauma in the Turkish mind.” Moscow also retains powerful leverage over Ankara, he suggested. Russia’s state nuclear company Rosatom is about to complete a multi-billion-dollar nuclear power station in Akkuyu, southern Turkey. Ankara sees it as vital to the drive to reduce its heavy dependence on imported energy. “It is illogical to oppose Russia now while you let the Russians complete the nuclear plant,” said Bagci. Erdogan hints at larger nuclear partnership with Russia, unsettling Turkey's allies Ankara also knows that letting NATO vessels in while barring Russian warships could provoke Moscow into contesting Turkey’s prized status as the gatekeeper to the Black Sea. However, retired Turkish diplomat Selim Kuneralp, an expert on the Montreux Convention, warns Turkey’s control over Black Sea access is likely already in Russian President Vladimir Putin ’s sights. “This has probably had an impact on Russia’s ability to conduct the war, and I doubt that Putin is very happy with the situation,” said Kuneralp. “So if he were to win the war, there is a very strong risk that he will take the initiative of saying: ‘this is unacceptable and we want to have free passage of warships from now on, regardless of whether there is a war’.” As a signatory, Moscow has the right to call for a revision of the Montreux Convention every five years. For centuries, Russia fought repeated wars with the then Ottoman Empire for control of the Turkish Straits. In the early years of the Cold War, even Joseph Stalin tried his hand , but the United States intervened and thwarted him. Now Ankara walks a tightrope between Moscow and its NATO partners to avoid a resurrection of those historical rivalries.
